name: Sophie Germain
who: A French girl who taught herself mathematics from her father's books
story: Sophie Germain lived in Paris more than 200 years ago. As a teenager she began reading the books in her father's library, and she taught herself Latin and Greek so that she could read even more of them. Her parents were not happy about it, but she kept learning. Later she wrote to famous mathematicians using a man's name, M. Le Blanc. One of them, the great mathematician Gauss, praised her ideas about numbers, and he went on praising her after he found out who she really was. Sophie was fascinated by prime numbers, which have exactly two factors: 1 and themselves. She studied primes p where 2 times p plus 1 is also prime. Today these are called Sophie Germain primes. She also won a prize from the Paris Academy of Sciences for her work on how thin metal plates vibrate.
link_to_lesson: Today you hunt for factors, and Sophie studied prime numbers, the numbers with only two factors.

try_it.q: Take 7. Is 2 times 7 plus 1 a prime? List the factors of your answer to prove it. Then try 5.
try_it.a: 2 x 7 + 1 = 15. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15, so 15 is not prime and 7 is not a Sophie Germain prime. For 5: 2 x 5 + 1 = 11, whose only factors are 1 and 11, so 11 is prime and 5 is a Sophie Germain prime.

icon_idea: A stack of old books with a small key tag showing 2p+1 on a number card (a pen-name mask is optional); not a portrait.

name: Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci)
country_or_region: Italy (Pisa), schooled in Bugia, now Bejaia, Algeria
who: An Italian merchant's son who helped Europe learn the digits 0 to 9
story: Leonardo of Pisa, whom we now call Fibonacci, lived about 800 years ago. His father was a merchant official who worked in Bugia, a trading town in North Africa that is now Bejaia in Algeria. Leonardo went there as a boy and learned to count with ten digits, 0 to 9, where each digit's place gives its value. In 1202 he finished a book, the Liber Abaci, which showed Italian merchants how to use these digits for money, trade and bookkeeping. Before that, many people in Europe wrote numbers with Roman numerals, which have no place value and no zero. Place value is what lets ten digits write any big number, such as 47 305. Leonardo did not invent these digits, but his book helped them spread across Europe.
link_to_lesson: Today you read and build numbers up to 100 000, and place value is the idea that Leonardo's book helped spread.

try_it.q: Use the digits 7, 0, 4, 9 and 2 once each. Write the biggest 5-digit number and the smallest 5-digit number you can.
try_it.a: Biggest: 97 420. Smallest: 20 479 (the 0 cannot go first, or it would not be a 5-digit number).

icon_idea: Ten digit tiles 0 to 9 sitting in labelled place-value columns, with a small merchant's scale beside them.

name: Katherine Johnson
who: A NASA mathematician who checked space-flight calculations
story: Katherine Johnson grew up in West Virginia in the USA. She was so quick at school that she was moved up several grades. She became a research mathematician at NASA's Langley centre in Virginia, where early on people who did calculations were called computers. She worked out the flight path for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight, the first American in space. In 1962 astronaut John Glenn was about to orbit the Earth. NASA now had electronic computers, but accounts say Glenn asked for Katherine to check the machine's numbers by hand. Her answers matched, and that helped everyone trust the plan. Checking an answer a second way is a habit every mathematician uses. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.
link_to_lesson: Today you use add, subtract, multiply and divide, and Katherine's job was to get these calculations right and to check them.

try_it.q: Check that 6 x 48 = 288 using a different method from the one you first used. (Hint: 48 is close to 50.)
try_it.a: 6 x 50 = 300, and 6 x 2 = 12, so 6 x 48 = 300 - 12 = 288. It checks out. You can also check with division: 288 divided by 6 = 48.

legend_note: Accounts say John Glenn asked for her to check the numbers. The exact timing is uncertain and the film Hidden Figures dramatised the scene, so do not describe it as in the film.
icon_idea: A pencil resting on a sheet with a big green tick beside a column of sums, and a small looping orbit path drawn above it.

name: Ahmes
years: about 1550 BC (the date of his copy of the papyrus)
who: An Egyptian scribe who copied a maths book on papyrus
story: About 3,500 years ago in Egypt, a scribe named Ahmes wrote out a long maths book on a roll of papyrus. We call it the Rhind Papyrus, named after the man who bought it in Luxor in 1858. Ahmes copied it from an older work. The book has problems about bread, fields and sharing. It also has a big table that writes fractions with 2 on top, such as 2 out of 3, 2 out of 5 and 2 out of 7, by using unit fractions, which have 1 on top. The table goes all the way up to 2 out of 101. A scribe's table like this saved time, because people could look up an answer instead of working it out every time. Parts of the papyrus are now kept in the British Museum in London.
link_to_lesson: Today you work with fractions, and Ahmes's papyrus shows people sharing and writing fractions 3,500 years ago.

try_it.q: Egyptian scribes liked unit fractions. Write 5/8 as two different unit fractions added together. (Hint: start with 1/2.)

icon_idea: A rolled papyrus scroll with the fractions 1/2 and 1/4 drawn on it in a simple reed-pen style, plus a small bread-loaf cut into pieces.

name: Simon Stevin
who: A Flemish mathematician who wrote a short book to teach decimals to everyone
story: Simon Stevin was born in Bruges, in what is now Belgium, in 1548. He worked on many things, from trigonometry to the science of water and weights. In 1585 he published a small book called The Tenth (La Thiende) about decimal fractions. Stevin did not invent decimals. Mathematicians in the Arab world and in China had used them before. What he did was explain them clearly for the people who needed them. He said they would be useful for surveyors, carpet-makers, wine-gaugers, mint-masters, stargazers and every kind of merchant. His idea was that if you divide everything into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, sums with money and measures become much easier. This is why we still use decimals for money and for measuring today.
link_to_lesson: Today you work with tenths, hundredths and thousandths, which is exactly what Stevin's small book explained.

try_it.q: Write 3 + 4/10 + 5/100 as a decimal. Then add 2.8 to your answer.

icon_idea: A ruler marked in tenths with a bold decimal point, next to a small tape measure and a coin; not a portrait.

name: Eratosthenes
country_or_region: Cyrene (now Libya) and Alexandria, Egypt; ancient Greek world
who: A Greek scholar who used a shadow angle to measure the Earth
story: Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who worked in the great library of Alexandria in Egypt, over 2,000 years ago. He heard that at noon on one day of the year the Sun shone straight down a deep well in the town of Syene, so nothing had a shadow. On that same day in Alexandria, a tall upright stick did make a shadow. Eratosthenes worked out that the shadow's angle was about 7.2 degrees, which is one fiftieth of a whole turn. That told him the two towns were one fiftieth of the way round the Earth. People had measured the distance between them as about 5,000 stadia, so he multiplied by 50. His answer, about 250,000 stadia, was surprisingly close to the real size. Historians cannot be sure how long his stadion was, so we cannot say exactly how close.
link_to_lesson: Today you measure angles and turns, and Eratosthenes used the angle of a shadow to measure the whole Earth.

try_it.q: A whole turn is 360 degrees. If a shadow made an angle of 10 degrees, how many angles that size would fit all the way round?
try_it.a: 360 divided by 10 = 36, so 36 angles. (Eratosthenes had about 7.2 degrees, and 360 divided by 7.2 = 50.)

legend_note: The exact length of a stadion is uncertain, so how close his answer was is uncertain too.
icon_idea: An upright stick on flat ground casting a short shadow, with a sun and a small angle arc drawn between the stick and a sunbeam.

name: Liu Hui
years: lived in the 3rd century AD (exact dates unknown)
who: A Chinese mathematician who explained why old area rules work
story: Very little is known about Liu Hui's life, except that he lived in China in the 3rd century AD. What we do know is his work. China had an old maths book called The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art. Its first chapter gives rules for finding the area of fields shaped like rectangles, triangles, trapeziums and circles. Liu Hui wrote notes on the book. He did not just say, use this rule. He worked to show why each rule gives the right answer, and he often did it with careful pictures and reasoning about shapes. That asking why is a big part of being a mathematician. When you explain why length times width gives the area of a rectangle, you are doing what Liu Hui did.
link_to_lesson: Today you find the area of rectangles and squares, and Liu Hui explained why the area rules for fields work.

try_it.q: A rectangular field is 12 m long and 5 m wide. Find its area and its perimeter. Then explain why the area rule works using rows of squares.
try_it.a: Area = 12 x 5 = 60 square metres. Perimeter = 12 + 5 + 12 + 5 = 34 m. The field is 5 rows of 12 squares, so the squares can be counted as 5 groups of 12, which is 60.

icon_idea: A brush pen beside a bamboo scroll showing a small field drawn as a rectangle on a square grid.

name: Emmy Noether
who: A German mathematician who found a link between symmetry and things that stay the same
story: Emmy Noether was born in Erlangen, Germany, in 1882. When she wanted to study mathematics at university, women were only allowed to sit in on classes if the teacher gave permission. She kept going, and in 1907 she earned her doctorate. For years she worked without pay. Later, she was invited to Gottingen, where for a time her lectures had to be advertised under another professor's name. Still she carried on, and her students admired her. In 1918 she proved a famous idea now called Noether's theorem. It says that when something in nature has a kind of symmetry, there is a matching quantity that stays the same. One example is that energy stays the same when the rules do not change over time. Symmetry is not only pretty. It tells us deep things.
link_to_lesson: Today you explore symmetry, and Emmy showed that symmetry is useful as well as beautiful.

try_it.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? How many does a rectangle that is not a square have?
try_it.a: A square has 4 lines of symmetry (2 through the middles of opposite sides and 2 along the diagonals). A rectangle that is not a square has 2 (through the middles of opposite sides).

icon_idea: A butterfly with matching wings and a dotted mirror line down the middle, sitting on a small chalkboard.

name: Florence Nightingale
who: A British nurse who used charts to show people what the numbers meant
story: Florence Nightingale was born in Florence, Italy, in 1820, and grew up in England. She is best known as a nurse, but she also loved numbers and statistics. During the Crimean War in the 1850s she collected figures about the hospitals for soldiers. They showed that many more soldiers became sick from dirty, crowded conditions than from the fighting. She knew that long lists of numbers are hard to read, so she drew special charts to make the facts easy to see. Her ideas helped to bring in cleaner, safer hospitals. In 1858 she became the first woman to be elected a Fellow of the Statistical Society of London, now called the Royal Statistical Society. She showed that a clear table or graph can help people make better decisions.
link_to_lesson: Today you read tables and line graphs, and Florence used tables and charts to make numbers easy to understand.

try_it.q: A table shows the temperature: 9 am 26 degrees, 12 noon 31 degrees, 3 pm 33 degrees, 6 pm 29 degrees. Between which two times did it rise the most, and by how much?
try_it.a: 9 am to 12 noon: it rose by 5 degrees (31 - 26). Noon to 3 pm: it rose by only 2 degrees. So the biggest rise was 9 am to 12 noon, by 5 degrees. (Between 3 pm and 6 pm it fell by 4 degrees.)

icon_idea: A small oil lamp beside a simple line graph with a rising and falling line, drawn in friendly flat colours; not a portrait.

name: Maryam Mirzakhani
who: An Iranian mathematician who loved hard problems and took her time over them
story: Maryam Mirzakhani grew up in Tehran, Iran. She loved solving maths problems, and she was the first girl to join Iran's team at the International Mathematical Olympiad, a competition for school students from around the world. She won a gold medal in 1994. She went back in 1995, got a perfect score, and won gold again. Later she studied at Harvard University in the USA and became a professor at Stanford University. She has been described as a slow thinker who took time with each problem, trying things out and making pictures of what might be going on. Her work on hard problems about shapes won her the Fields Medal in 2014. She was the first woman to win it. Her story shows that patience and trying different ways in can solve big problems.
link_to_lesson: Today you choose a strategy for tricky puzzles, and Maryam became a champion by being patient and trying new ways in.

try_it.q: A farmer has hens (2 legs) and rabbits (4 legs). There are 5 animals and 14 legs in all. How many of each? Try guess and check, or suppose they are all hens.
try_it.a: 3 hens and 2 rabbits. Check: 3 x 2 + 2 x 4 = 6 + 8 = 14 legs and 3 + 2 = 5 animals. (If all 5 were hens there would be 10 legs. The extra 4 legs mean 2 animals are rabbits, since each rabbit adds 2 extra legs.)

icon_idea: A gold-coloured medal beside a notebook page with a path of loops and arrows drawn inside a polygon; not a portrait.
